paragraphs: The doctor came out of the room again, bundled up in his fur coat with his cap on his head. His face looked almost angry and disgusted, as if he were afraid of getting dirty. He gave the passage a quick glance, looking sternly at Alyosha and Kolya as he did so. Alyosha waved from the door to the coachman, and the carriage that had brought the doctor pulled up. The captain darted out after the doctor and, bowing apologetically, stopped him to get one last word. The poor man looked completely crushed, and there was a scared look in his eyes.

“Your Excellency, your Excellency ... is it possible?” he began, but could not go on and clasped his hands in despair. Even so, he kept gazing at the doctor, pleading, as though one word from him might still change the poor boy’s fate.
“I can’t help it, I’m not God!” the doctor answered offhandedly, though with his usual air of importance.
“Doctor ... your Excellency ... will it be soon, soon?”
“You must be prepared for anything,” said the doctor in emphatic, cutting tones, and, lowering his eyes, he was about to step out to the carriage.
“Your Excellency, for Christ’s sake!” the terrified captain stopped him again. “Your Excellency! But can nothing, absolutely nothing save him now?”

“It’s not in my hands now,” said the doctor impatiently, “but, h’m!...” he stopped suddenly. “If you could, for instance ... send ... your patient ... at once, without delay” (the doctor said the words “at once, without delay” with an almost angry sternness that made the captain start) “to Syracuse, the change to the new be-ne-ficial climate might possibly have an effect—”
“To Syracuse!” cried the captain, unable to take in what was said.
“Syracuse is in Sicily,” Kolya jerked out suddenly by way of explanation. The doctor looked at him.
“Sicily! Your Excellency,” faltered the captain, “but you’ve seen”—he spread out his hands, pointing at his surroundings—“mamma and my family?”

“N—no, Sicily is no place for the family. The family should go to the Caucasus in early spring ... your daughter must go to the Caucasus, and your wife ... after a course of the waters in the Caucasus for her rheumatism ... must be sent straight to Paris, to the mental specialist Lepelletier. I could give you a note for him, and then ... there might be a change—”
“Doctor, doctor! But you see!” The captain flung his hands wide again in despair, pointing at the bare wooden walls of the passage.
“Well, that’s not my business,” grinned the doctor. “I’ve only told you what medical science answers to your question about possible treatment. As for the rest, to my regret—”

“Don’t be afraid, apothecary, my dog won’t bite you,” Kolya rapped out loudly, noticing the doctor’s rather uneasy glance at Perezvon, who was standing in the doorway. There was an angry note in Kolya’s voice. He said apothecary instead of doctor on purpose and, as he explained afterwards, said it “to insult him.”
“What’s that?” The doctor threw up his head, staring at Kolya in surprise. “Who is this?” he asked Alyosha, as though wanting him to explain.
“It’s Perezvon’s master. Don’t worry about me,” Kolya said sharply again.
“Perezvon?”[7] repeated the doctor, puzzled.
“He hears the bell, but where it is he cannot tell. Good-by, we’ll meet in Syracuse.”
“Who is this? Who is this?” The doctor flew into a terrible rage.

“He’s a schoolboy, doctor, a mischievous boy. Take no notice of him,” said Alyosha, frowning and speaking quickly. “Kolya, hold your tongue!” he cried to Krassotkin. “Take no notice of him, doctor,” he repeated, a little impatiently.
“He needs a thrashing, a good thrashing!” The doctor stamped his foot in a perfect fury.
“And you know, apothecary, my Perezvon might bite!” said Kolya, turning pale, his voice quivering and his eyes flashing. “_Ici_, Perezvon!”
“Kolya, if you say another word, I’ll have nothing more to do with you,” Alyosha cried in a commanding voice.
“There’s only one man in the world who can command Nikolay Krassotkin—this is the man”; Kolya pointed at Alyosha. “I obey him. Good-by!”

He stepped forward, opened the door and quickly went into the inner room. Perezvon flew after him. The doctor stood still for five seconds in amazement, looking at Alyosha. Then, with a curse, he went quickly out to the carriage, repeating aloud, “This is ... this is ... I don’t know what it is!” The captain darted forward to help him into the carriage. Alyosha followed Kolya into the room. Kolya was already at Ilusha’s bedside. The sick boy was holding his hand and calling for his father. A minute later the captain came back too.

“Father, father, come ... we ...” Ilusha faltered in violent excitement, but, apparently unable to go on, he flung his wasted arms around his father and Kolya, joining them in one embrace and hugging them as tightly as he could. The captain suddenly began to shake with silent sobs, and Kolya’s lips and chin twitched.
“Father, father! I’m so sorry for you!” Ilusha moaned bitterly.
“Ilusha ... darling ... the doctor said ... you would be all right ... we’ll be happy ... the doctor ...” the captain began.
“Ah, father! I know what the new doctor told you about me.... I saw!” cried Ilusha, and again he hugged them both with all his strength, hiding his face on his father’s shoulder.
“Father, don’t cry, and when I die, get a good boy, another one ... choose one from all of them, a good one, call him Ilusha and love him instead of me....”
“Hush, old man, you’ll get well,” Krassotkin cried suddenly, in a voice that sounded angry.

“But don’t ever forget me, father,” Ilusha went on, “come to my grave ... and, father, bury me by our big stone, where we used to go for our walk, and come to me there in the evening with Krassotkin ... and Perezvon ... I’ll be waiting for you.... Father, father!”
His voice broke. All three were silent, still embracing. Nina was crying quietly in her chair, and at last, seeing them all crying, “mamma” burst into tears too.
“Ilusha! Ilusha!” she exclaimed.
Krassotkin suddenly pulled himself out of Ilusha’s embrace.

“Good-by, old man, mother expects me back for dinner,” he said quickly. “What a pity I didn’t tell her! She’ll be dreadfully worried.... But after dinner I’ll come back to you for the whole day, the whole evening, and I’ll tell you all sorts of things, all sorts of things. And I’ll bring Perezvon, but now I’m taking him with me, because he’ll start howling when I’m away and bother you. Good-by!”
And he ran out into the passage. He didn’t want to cry, but in the passage he burst into tears. Alyosha found him crying.
“Kolya, you must be sure to keep your word and come, or he’ll be terribly disappointed,” Alyosha said emphatically.
“I will! Oh, how I curse myself for not coming before!” muttered Kolya, crying, and no longer ashamed of it.

At that moment the captain flew out of the room and shut the door behind him at once. His face looked frenzied, and his lips were trembling. He stood in front of the two of them and flung up his arms.

“I don’t want a good boy! I don’t want another boy!” he muttered in a wild whisper, clenching his teeth. “If I forget thee, Jerusalem, may my tongue—” He broke off with a sob and sank to his knees before the wooden bench. Pressing his fists against his head, he began sobbing with absurd whimpering cries, doing all he could to keep them from being heard in the room.
Kolya ran out into the street.
“Good-by, Karamazov? Will you come yourself?” he cried sharply and angrily to Alyosha.
“I’ll certainly come in the evening.”
“What was that he said about Jerusalem?... What did he mean by that?”
“It’s from the Bible. ‘If I forget thee, Jerusalem,’ that is, if I forget everything most precious to me, if I let anything take its place, then may—”
“I understand, that’s enough! Make sure you come! _Ici_, Perezvon!” he cried with real ferocity to the dog, and with rapid strides he went home.
